h: The Quiet Cry That Rectifies the Root

p: בַּזֹּהַר הַקָּדוֹשׁ עַל פָּסוּק וְהַקֹּל נִשְׁמַע וְגוֹמֵר אִיתָא דְּאִצְטְרִיךְ לְצַלָּאָה בְּלַחַשׁ בְּהַהוּא קָלָא דְּלָא אִשְׁתְּמַע וְדָא הִיא צְלוֹתָא דְּאִתְקַבְּלַת תָּדִיר וְסִימָנָיךְ וְהַקֹּל נִשְׁמַע קֹל בְּלֹא וָא״ו נִשְׁמַע.

— The holy Zohar teaches concerning ‘The voice was heard,’ etc., that one must pray quietly, with that voice which is not heard; this is the prayer that is always accepted. Its sign is ‘The voice was heard’: kol, written without vav, is heard.
וּלְהָבִין זֹאת דְּהָא כְתִיב אָכֵן שָׁמַע אֱלֹהִים הִקְשִׁיב בְּקוֹל תְּפִלָּתִי וְכָתוּב בְּקוֹל בְּוָא״ו.
— To understand this: is it not written, ‘But God has heard; He has attended to the voice of my prayer,’ with bekol spelled with a vav?

אָכֵן אֵין הַמְכוּוָּן בָּזֶה עַל הַקּוֹל הֲבָרָה הַנִּשְׁמָע לְאָזְנֵי הָאָדָם רַק הַצְּעָקָה הַיּוֹצֵא מִפְּנִימִיּוּת נְקוּדָּה שֶׁבַּלֵּב וְאֵין לָהּ הֲבָנָה בִּתְפִיסַת הָאָדָם זוּלַת לְהַיּוֹדֵעַ תַּעֲלוּמוֹת הַלֵּב וּכְמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב וּשְׁמַע צַעֲקָתֵנוּ יוֹדֵעַ תַּעֲלוּמוֹת

— The meaning is not an audible sound heard by human ears, but the cry emerging from the innermost point of the heart. It lies beyond human comprehension, known only to the One who knows the heart's secrets. As we say, ‘Hear our cry, Knower of hidden things.’
וְזֶהוּ קוֹל דִּבְלַחַשׁ דְּאִתְקַבְּלַת כִּי עַל יְדֵי זֶה נִתְקַן כָּל הַפְּגָמִים עַד הַשּׁוֹרֶשׁ.
— This is the quiet voice that is accepted, for through it all blemishes are rectified as far as their root.

paragraphs.text: Zohar I, 209b: “Therefore a person should not make his voice heard in prayer, but should pray in a whisper, with that voice which is not heard. This is the prayer that is always accepted. Your sign is “The voice was heard”: kol, written without a vav, is heard. This is prayer in silence, as it is written of Channah, “Her voice was not heard.” This is the prayer the Holy One, blessed be He, accepts when it is offered with desire, intention, and proper order, and to unify the unity of one’s Master properly every day.”

paragraphs.text: Parallel: Pri Tzaddik, Rosh Hashanah 9:1: “To understand the expression ‘Hear my voice’: did the Sages not say that one who makes his voice heard in his prayer is of those of little faith? … For with Hashem there is no difference even if one prays in a whisper, since He answers a whisper. Rather, the intent is the voice of a cry that emerges from the depths of the heart, until one cannot articulate it with his lips even in formed speech, but only cries out with a simple voice from the pain of his heart. Such a prayer is the most accepted, as it is said, ‘A prayer of the poor man when he is faint, and pours out his speech before Hashem.’ … This is the meaning of ‘Let Your ears be attentive to the voice of my supplications’: to the voice specifically, not to the supplications, for prayer requires a time of favor and is not answered at all times; but the voice of crying that issues from the groan of the depths of the heart is always heard, by virtue of the attribute of compassion before Him, blessed be He, who is called the merciful Father.”

paragraphs.text: Connection: Rosh Hashanah 9 asks the same question, how a verse can ask God to hear the voice when prayer is meant to be silent, and gives the same answer: a cry from the depth of the heart, beyond formed speech. It adds that such a cry is heard at every time, while worded supplication waits for a time of favor, which explains why this prayer ‘is always accepted.’

paragraphs.text: Parallel: Machshavot Charutz §11: “[The shofar] unites and joins the beginning of thought with the end of action. This occurs through the voice beyond speech and the actual articulation of letters, in which the letters of thought and the cry of the heart are revealed. Every thought in the heart must give rise to some voice indicating how deeply that thought is immersed and fixed. ‘The voice is Jacob’s voice’—his offspring were all complete—and in this voice the light is revealed that Israel arose in [God’s] thought. Even the sinners of Israel have a hold on this voice: at some point during their lives they utter a true cry to God from the depths of the heart, whether a voice of joy from love and recognition of His kindness and mercy, or a voice of groaning and wailing from awe and fear.”

p: וְאִיתָא (בְּמִדְרַשׁ תַּנְחוּמָא ה) וְהַקֹּל נִשְׁמַע וְאֵין קוֹל זֶה אֶלָּא קוֹל יְהוּדָה שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר שְׁמַע הַשֵּׁם קוֹל יְהוּדָה.
— It is taught (Midrash Tanchuma 5): ‘The voice was heard’—this voice is none other than Judah's voice, as it is said, ‘Hear, Hashem, the voice of Judah.’

כִּי בָזֶה שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר וַיִּגַּשׁ אֵלָיו יְהוּדָה וַיֹּאמֶר בִּי אֲדֹנִי הָיָה הַגָּשָׁה לִתְפִלָּה מֵעוֹמֶק הַלֵּב לְהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ (וּכְמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב בִּבְרֵאשִׁית רַבָּה וְנִתְבָּאֵר מַאֲמָר א) שֶׁאֵין לוֹ שׁוּם עֵצָה רַק שֶׁמְּצַפֶּה לִישׁוּעָתוֹ יִתְבָּרַךְ

— ‘Judah approached him and said: Please, my lord’ was an approach to prayer from the depth of his heart to Hashem (as taught in Bereishit Rabbah and explained in discourse 1): he had no recourse other than awaiting His blessed salvation.
וּבָזֶה הָיָה נִתְבָּרֵר לִהְיוֹת נִתְקַן גַּם הַשֹּׁרֶשׁ וְנַעֲשָׂה בָּזֶה הֲכָנָה לְכָל כְּלַל יִשְׂרָאֵל.
— Through this refinement, the root too was rectified, preparing the way for all Israel.

h: Gathering the Holy Sparks of Egypt

p: וְלָכֵן אַחַר שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר וְהַקֹּל נִשְׁמַע בָּא בְּפִי פַרְעֹה לוֹמַר וְאֶתְּנָה לָכֶם אֶת טוּב אֶרֶץ מִצְרַיִם נִבָּא וְאֵינוֹ יוֹדֵעַ מַה נִּבָּא (כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב רַבִּי שְׁלֹמֹה יִצְחָקִי)
— Therefore, after ‘The voice was heard,’ Pharaoh was moved to say, ‘I shall give you the good of the land of Egypt’—he prophesied without knowing what he prophesied, as Rashi explains.

כִּי כַּאֲשֶׁר בֶּאֱמֶת כְּבָר נִתְקַן הַשּׁוֹרֶשׁ אָזַי מִמֵּילָא נִתְלַקְּטִים כָּל הַנִּיצוֹצוֹת קְדוֹשׁוֹת אֲשֶׁר הֵם מְפוּזָּרִים בֵּין הַקְּלִיפּוֹת וְזֶה טוּב כָּל אֶרֶץ מִצְרַיִם דְּהַיְינוּ עֶצֶם הַחַיּוּת שֶׁלָּהֶם
— For once the root is truly rectified, all the holy sparks scattered among the husks of impurity are gathered in of themselves. This is the good of the whole land of Egypt: its very life-force.

וּמִמֵּילָא נִשְׁאֲרוּ בְּלֹא חַיּוּת וְעַל זֶה רָמַז גַּם כֵּן יוֹסֵף בַּפָּסוּק וּלְאָבִיו שָׁלַח כְּזֹאת עֶשֶׂר חֲמוֹרִים נוֹשְׂאִים מִטּוּב מִצְרַיִם וּבַגְּמָרָא (מְגִילָּה טז:) שָׁלַח לוֹ יַיִן יָשָׁן שֶׁדַּעַת זְקֵנִים נוֹחָה הֵימֶנּוּ

— Consequently they are left without vitality. Joseph also alluded to this in ‘To his father he sent as follows: ten donkeys carrying the good of Egypt.’ The Talmud (Megillah 16b) explains that he sent aged wine, with which elders are pleased.
וְהַיְינוּ חֲמַר עַתִּיק דְּאַף עַל גַּב דְּהוּא שָׁתֵי לֵיהּ טַעְמָא וְרֵיחָא בְּפוּמֵיהּ (כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב שִׁיר הַשִּׁירִים רַבָּה פָּרָשָׁה ז וְנִתְבָּאֵר מַאֲמָר ט)
— This is aged wine, whose taste and aroma remain in his mouth even after he drinks it, as stated in Shir HaShirim Rabbah, chapter 7, and explained in discourse 9.
וְהַיְינוּ תִּיקּוּן הַשּׁוֹרֶשׁ עַל יְדֵי בְּחִינַת עַתִּיקָא וְעַל יְדֵי זֶה נִלְקָטִים כָּל הַנִּיצוֹצוֹת הַקְּדוֹשׁוֹת שֶׁזֶּהוּ טוּב מִצְרַיִם כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמַרְנוּ:
— It signifies the rectification of the root through the aspect of Atika; thereby all the holy sparks are gathered in. This is Egypt's goodness, as we explained.

paragraphs.text: Megillah 16b: ““To his father he sent the following: ten donkeys carrying the good of Egypt.” What is “the good of Egypt”? Rabbi Binyamin bar Yefet said in Rabbi Elazar’s name: He sent him aged wine, which is pleasing to the minds of elders.”

paragraphs.text: Bereshit 45:23: “To his father he sent the following: ten donkeys carrying the good things of Egypt, and ten female donkeys carrying grain, bread, and food for his father on the journey.”

paragraphs.text: Shir HaShirim Rabbah 7:10: ““Making the lips of sleepers move”: Rabbi Yochanan ben Torta said: Even after he has died, his lips move in the grave. What is the reason? “Making the lips of sleepers move.” Shmuel said: Like a vat of grapes that flows of itself. Rabbi Chanina bar Pappa and Rabbi Simon differed: one said, like someone drinking spiced wine; the other said, like someone drinking aged wine—even after he has drunk it, its taste and fragrance remain in his mouth.”
